memories.title: Obelisk of Theodosius
memories.summary: A 3,500-year-old Egyptian obelisk, carved for Thutmose III and shipped to Constantinople by Theodosius I.
details: About 19 m tall today. Only the top third survived the journey, so it once stood nearly 30 m.
The Roman marble base shows Theodosius and his family watching the races. A Greek inscription runs across the lower block.
The hieroglyphs on the shaft are still crisp.

media.alt: The Obelisk of Theodosius with a Blue Mosque minaret rising behind it
The marble base of the obelisk, carved with Theodosius and his court watching the races

memories.title: Hagia Sophia
memories.summary: Justinian’s cathedral of Holy Wisdom, built in under six years, and an Ottoman mosque from 1453. Seen from outside; the inside is saved for another day.
details: The dome is about 31 m wide and 55 m high. In your photo it is wrapped in scaffolding.
Still to find inside: the Deësis mosaic, the Omphalion in the floor, the Weeping Column and the Viking graffiti.
Cathedral, then mosque, then a museum from 1935, and a mosque again since 2020.

media.alt: Hagia Sophia seen across the park, with scaffolding around the dome

memories.title: Blue Mosque
memories.summary: Sultan Ahmed I’s mosque, lined with more than 20,000 hand-painted İznik tiles.
details: Six minarets was unusual for the time. The popular story says the architect heard altı (six) when the sultan asked for altın (gold).
An iron chain over the courtyard door made even a mounted sultan lower his head.
It is an active mosque, so visits pause at prayer times.

media.alt: The Blue Mosque courtyard with its arcade, cascading domes and tall minarets under a grey sky
Selfie of Wei and Szu Ker in the Blue Mosque courtyard with the domes and minarets behind
The Blue Mosque courtyard, domes and two minarets under grey cloud

memories.title: Basilica Cistern
memories.summary: A sunken Byzantine water store, about 138 m by 65 m, held up by 336 marble columns.
details: Two columns in the far corner rest on Medusa heads, one sideways and one upside down. Nobody knows why. Coins cover the floor around the upside-down one.
Forgotten for centuries, until Petrus Gyllius traced it in 1545 after locals pulled fish up through their basement floors.
Carp swim in the shallow water. It also appears in From Russia with Love.

media.alt: An upside-down Medusa head at the foot of a column in the Basilica Cistern, with coins scattered around it
An upside-down Medusa head at the base of a column, coins in the water around it
Rows of lit columns reflected in the water of the cistern

memories.title: Süleymaniye Mosque
memories.summary: Sinan’s mosque for Suleiman the Magnificent, on the highest of the seven hills above the Golden Horn.
details: Four minarets carry ten balconies, a nod to Suleiman being the tenth Ottoman sultan.
Air channels carried candle soot to a room above the entrance, where it was collected for ink.
Suleiman and Hürrem Sultan rest in the garden tombs. Sinan’s own modest tomb sits just outside the north wall.

media.alt: Clip panning over the grey lead domes of the Süleymaniye Mosque toward the Galata Tower and the city under heavy cloud

memories.title: Dagger & Spoonmaker’s Diamond
memories.summary: Two stars of the Imperial Treasury: a dagger set with emeralds, and an 86-carat diamond.
details: The dagger was made in 1747 as a gift for Nader Shah of Persia. He was assassinated before it arrived, so it stayed in Istanbul.
A fourth emerald on the pommel opens to reveal a small watch. The dagger inspired the 1964 film Topkapi.
The diamond’s label says it was most likely acquired under Mehmed IV (r. 1648–1687) and is ringed by 49 smaller diamonds. The spoonmaker story is a legend.
Outside the treasury, the palace terraces and gardens look over the Bosphorus and the Golden Horn.

media.alt: The Spoonmaker’s Diamond glowing in its dark display case, with the museum label below
The Topkapı Dagger in its case, its hilt set with large emeralds and its sheath with diamonds
Wei and Szu Ker on a marble terrace with the Bosphorus behind
Selfie of Szu Ker and Wei in the palace garden with the Galata skyline behind

memories.title: The Harem
memories.summary: The sultan’s family quarters, about 400 rooms, run in practice by his mother, the Valide Sultan.
details: Murad III’s Privy Chamber, designed by Sinan, is the showpiece: İznik tiles, a wall fountain and a gilded dome.
The Cage kept princes under tight watch to head off challenges to the throne.
It needs a separate ticket, and the route is one-way.

memories.title: Sahaflar Book Bazaar
memories.summary: Open-air second-hand booksellers under plane trees, with books laid out on the ground between the stalls.

memories.title: Galata Tower at night

memories.title: Kadıköy
memories.summary: Across the Bosphorus for the fish market, with whole bonito stacked head-up and the gills flared red.
details: The stall sign reads Cihan Balık. Palamut is bonito.

media.alt: Rows of bonito with red gills on a fish market stall

memories.title: Mayko Lokanta
memories.summary: A warm, red-seated restaurant: bread, meze and a bottle of ayran.
details: This was the favourite dinner of the trip.

media.alt: Wei at a restaurant table with meze, bread and a bottle of ayran

memories.title: Balık dürüm
memories.summary: The famous fish wrap, eaten on the first day after the book market and the Süleymaniye. A short clip of the first bites.
details: Balık dürüm is grilled or fried fish wrapped in thin flatbread with salad.
Filmed at a street-side table with stone walls behind.

media.alt: Szu Ker in a blue puffer jacket eating a balık dürüm wrap held in paper at a street-side table
